sections.html: Two Megalancistrus were imported from Paraguay, from the Rio Urguayo. They are currently 40-50 cm long and show clearly why they deserve their generic name: Megalancistrus means "gigantic Ancistrus".

L113, Megalancistrus parananus, is a large suckermouth catfish from the rios Paraná, Paraguay and Uruguay in Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay and Argentina. It was formerly thought to include L234, but only L113 appears native to these drainages, while L234 comes from the rio São Francisco. The largest recorded specimen measured 588 mm, and it can behave very aggressively in confined surroundings.

  • Needs a tank at least 2 m long
Imported from Paraguay, from the Rio Urguayo.

Distributed throughout the rios Paraná, Paraguay and Uruguay in southern Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay, and Argentina.

Type locality is 'Río Paraná at La Paz, Entre-Ríos, Argentina'.

Standard length: 58.8 cm SL.

Suitable only for public installations or the very largest private aquaria.

Intestinal analyses of wild specimens have shown it to feed chiefly on freshwater sponges and other aquatic invertebrates alongside smaller quantities of wood, although it's unclear whether the latter is an essential part of the diet or ingested unintentionally while the fish are foraging.

In the aquarium it does best when offered a varied diet comprising sinking dried foods, frozen Daphnia, mosquito larvae, chironomid larvae (bloodworm), and prawn/shrimp, for example, plus fresh fruit, parboiled potato, etc.

Home-made foods using a mixture of natural ingredients bound with gelatin are very useful since they can be tailored to contain fresh vegetables, Spirulina and meatier ingredients.
Can behave very aggressively in confined surroundings and should only be maintained alongside similarly-sized, robust fishes in suitably-sized aquaria (see 'Aquarium Size').
Scientifically speaking, these fish most probably belong to the species M. parananus.

Etymology: Megalancistrus comes from the Greek μέγας (mégas), meaning 'big, large, great', and the generic name Ancistrus. parananus is named for the Río Paraná, type locality of the species.

This species was formerly considered to be represented by the L-numbers L113 and L234 but it appears that only the former is native to the Paraná, Paraguay and Uruguay drainages, whereas L234 is collected in the rio São Francisco in eastern Brazil.

M. barrae and M. sp. 'LDA097' are also exported from the São Francisco system.

  • Reis, R. E., S. O. Kullander and C. J. Ferraris, Jr. (eds) (2003). Check list of the freshwater fishes of South and Central America. CLOFFSCA. EDIPUCRS, Porto Alegre, i-xi + 1-729
  • Stawikowski, R., A. Werner and I. Seidel (2004). DATZ Special: L-Numbers. DATZ, 1-132
Brazil: Paraguay, Paraná and Uruguay River basins. Type locality: Paraná River at La Paz in Entre Ríos, Argentina.
Will need a very large aquarium as they are a territorial species and will also need hiding places such as driftwood and large caves.
Omnivore. Frozen foods such as brine shrimp, mosquito larvae, shrimps, mussels and fish flesh, as well as good quality dried foods. They will also eat green foods in the aquarium.
Males have a broader head, longer pectoral fins, a slender body and longer odontodes, especially around the gill cover area.

Megalancistrus is closely related to Pseudacanthicus and, in both sexes, the body is covered in spiny odontodes, but Megalancistrus has more soft rays in the dorsal fin (between 10 and 12).

Etymology: the specific name parananus refers to the Rio Paraná, Brazil.

IUCN Red List: despite the little information available on this species, it has a wide range and no apparent threats. It is therefore assessed as Least Concern (LC) (IUCN 2023).
